subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Defining Life
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Defining Life.

hook.text: We're searching the universe for life, but scientists still can't fully agree on what life actually is.

buildup.text: NASA defines it as a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution. But edge cases challenge every definition.

discovery.text: Viruses replicate but can't sustain themselves. Fire grows and consumes energy. Neither is alive by most definitions.

twist.text: If alien life uses completely different chemistry, our Earth-based definitions might not recognize it at all.

climax.text: The search forces us to think broadly. We look for chemistry, energy use, and complexity—not just familiar biology.

punchline.text: We can't fully define life—yet we're searching the cosmos for it.

quiz.question: Why is defining life difficult for the search for extraterrestrial life?
options: Alien life might use completely different chemistry that our definitions wouldn't recognize
All definitions of life require DNA, which only exists on Earth
Life can only exist in liquid water environments

details.summary: Defining life is surprisingly difficult — biologists use criteria like metabolism, reproduction, response to stimuli, and evolution, but edge cases (viruses, fire, crystals) challenge every definition.
details.whyItMatters: Without a clear definition of life, we risk designing detectors that only find Earth-like biology. A broader definition guides the search for truly alien organisms that may operate on completely different chemistry.
takeaways: No single definition of life satisfies all edge cases
Criteria include metabolism, reproduction, and evolution
The definition we choose shapes what instruments we build

faq.question: Why are viruses hard to classify as alive?
faq.answer: Viruses reproduce and evolve but cannot metabolize or replicate independently — they hijack host cells. They satisfy some life criteria but not others. This ambiguity makes viruses a key test case for any proposed definition of life.

faq.question: What is NASA's working definition of life?
faq.answer: NASA defines life as a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution. This broad definition avoids Earth-centric assumptions while requiring the two key features — self-maintenance and adaptation — that most biologists consider essential.
